# The Value of Disagreement: Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

## Rethinking What a Successful Meeting Looks Like

There is a common assumption, woven deep into workplace culture, that a good meeting is one where everyone leaves nodding. The room reaches agreement, heads bob, someone volunteers to "circle back," and everyone walks out feeling productive. But this picture of success deserves scrutiny. Agreement, it turns out, can be a mirage. It can conceal genuine uncertainty, paper over unexamined assumptions, and postpone conflicts that will only grow more expensive with time.

A truly productive meeting might end quite differently: not with everyone agreeing, but with everyone able to state precisely what they disagree about, what evidence would settle the question, and who is responsible for gathering that evidence. This is a harder standard than it sounds. It requires participants to be honest about their doubts, articulate about their reasoning, and disciplined about what would change their minds. But meetings that achieve this are worth far more than meetings that achieve superficial harmony.

## The Hidden Cost of False Consensus

Consider a familiar scenario. A product team meets to decide whether to launch a new feature. The engineering lead has reservations about technical debt but doesn't want to seem obstructionist.
